summary: A Bank of America team led by economist Jeseo Park argues that today's housing market resembles the early 1980s rather than the 2008 crash. High mortgage rates are slowing sales while prices hold up, supported by low inventory and millennial demand. The team warns of more near-term 'turbulence' but does not expect a 2008-style crash.
one_line: Bank of America says the current housing slowdown mirrors the 1980s, with stalled sales but resilient prices, not a repeat of the 2008 crash.
key_facts: Bank of America economist Jeseo Park and her team wrote in a Thursday note that the 1980s are a better analogy for today's housing market than the 2008 crash.
National home prices peaked in June 2022, fell more than 5% by January 2023, then returned to a record high in July.
Mortgage rates hit a 23-year high in October 2023; the average 30-year fixed rate rose from 3.8% in March 2022 to over 7.5%.
Household mortgage debt was roughly 65% of disposable income in Q2 2023, versus 100% before the GFC.
Loan-to-value was 27% in Q2 2023, versus over 40% in 2008 and roughly 50% in 2010.
Adjustable-rate mortgages are under 5% of purchase and refinance loans, compared with over 35% at the pre-GFC peak.
CPI inflation peaked around 14% in 1980, and Paul Volcker's policies sent mortgage rates to 18% within a year, sparking a recession.
In the early 1980s home sales and building cratered, but prices stayed stable: the median price was $64,700 in August 1979 and $69,400 by Q2 1981.
Favorable demographics supported the 1980s market (baby boomers) and today's (millennials reaching prime homebuying age).
Bank of America says low existing-home inventory plus millennial demand could create a 'floor beneath home prices'.
Bank of America previously forecast 0% home price growth and falling home sales for 2023 and gave no new forecast in this note.
The team says affordability will improve once inflation fades and the Fed cuts rates: 'Until then, hang tight, it may be a bumpy ride.'
